hints: Trace the root from outside to inside: epidermis (4) is outermost, then cortex cell walls (2), then endodermis with its Casparian strip (3 and 1), then xylem (5) in the centre. Which options move in that outside to inside order?

Remember the Casparian strip is a waterproof band of suberin that blocks the apoplast pathway in the walls. Water in the walls (2) cannot go through (1), it must divert into the living endodermal cells (3).
walkthrough:
**Map the root from outside to inside**

Think of water entering a root like travelling inward. The order is epidermal cells on the outside, then cell walls of the cortex cells, then the endodermis, then xylem vessels in the centre.

So a correct sequence must generally go 4 to 2 to 3 to 5.

**Remember what the Casparian strip does**

Water can move through cell walls by the apoplast pathway. But at the endodermis, the Casparian strip (1) is waterproof and seals the walls.

This means water in the cortex cell walls (2) cannot continue in the walls through (1). It must enter the cytoplasm of the endodermal cells (3) by the symplast pathway.

**Check which sequence is actually possible**

Option A shows 2 to 3 to 5. That is cortex walls, then into endodermal cells to get around the block, then on to xylem. That is exactly what happens in a real root.

Any sequence that tries to go straight through the Casparian strip in the walls, or goes backwards, cannot happen.

options.A: Correct. Water in the apoplast of the cortex walls (2) enters the endodermal cells (3) to bypass the Casparian strip, then passes to the xylem (5).
options.B: False. Water in the cell walls (2) cannot move directly through the Casparian strip (1) because it is impermeable to water.
options.C: False. Although 4 to 2 is correct, the pathway then stops at the Casparian strip (1) which blocks further movement in the walls.
options.D: False. This order is backwards, water cannot go from endodermal cells (3) outward back to cortex walls (2) when moving across to the xylem.
